what: The Social Media Character Counter shows, as you type, how much of each app's limit your text uses: X posts, Instagram captions, TikTok captions, YouTube titles and descriptions, Facebook and LinkedIn posts, Pinterest pin titles and descriptions, and Threads posts.

It counts characters the way people see them, so a flag or a family emoji counts as one character, and it follows X's own weighting rules, where links count as 23 and emoji and Chinese, Japanese or Korean characters count as 2. It also counts hashtags, @mentions, links, words and lines.
A "Copy for Instagram" button keeps your blank lines when you paste into Instagram, which normally squashes paragraphs together. Your text stays in your browser.
uses: See the real weighted count so a post with links and emoji does not get cut off at 280.
Check the 2,200-character limit, the 30-hashtag and 20-mention limits, and keep paragraph spacing.
Keep titles within 100 characters and descriptions within 5,000, and spot banned < > characters.
See where the text folds behind "see more" so your hook is in the first lines.
Write one text and check it against every platform at once.
tutorial: Click the "Your post or caption" box and type or paste your text. All counters update instantly.
The boxes under the text show characters, words, hashtags, mentions, links and lines.
Each row shows used / limit, a bar, and how many characters are left. The bar turns orange at 90% and red when you are over the limit or break a rule.
X counts differently. Each link counts as 23 whatever its length, every emoji counts as 2, and letters from scripts like Chinese or Japanese count as 2. The number in the X row already includes this.
Red notes under a row tell you about too many hashtags or mentions for Instagram, or characters YouTube does not accept.
Click "Copy text" to copy it as it is, or "Copy for Instagram (keep blank lines)" to add invisible spacers to empty lines so Instagram keeps your paragraphs.
features: X, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube title and description, Facebook, LinkedIn, Pinterest title and description, and Threads.
Implements the open twitter-text rules: links as 23, emoji as 2, wide characters as 2.
Uses grapheme clusters so complex emoji count as one character.
Warns when Instagram's 30-hashtag or 20-mention limits are passed.
Shows where Instagram, LinkedIn, Facebook and YouTube cut text behind "more".
Copies with invisible spacer characters so blank lines survive.
Nothing you type leaves your device.

example.title: Worked example: one launch post, three apps
example.text: You write a 240-character announcement with two emoji and the link https://example.com/spring-collection-2025. The Characters box says 240, but the X row shows 224 / 280 because the 41-character link counts as 23 and each emoji adds 1 extra. The LinkedIn row says the text folds after about 210 characters, so you move the key offer into the first sentence. You add blank lines between paragraphs and click "Copy for Instagram (keep blank lines)" before pasting into Instagram.

tips: Put your hook in the first 125 characters for Instagram and the first 210 for LinkedIn, before the "more" link.
On X, a long link costs no more than a short one, so there is no need to shorten links just to save characters.
Emoji count as 2 on X, so a row of emoji uses up the limit faster than you might think.
Use the Instagram copy button whenever your caption has paragraphs or lists.
Keep YouTube titles under about 70 characters so they are not cut off in search results.
Limits change from time to time. If an app rejects a post that fits here, trust the app.
problems: The X count is higher than the character count
That is expected. X counts emoji and some scripts as 2 and every link as 23. The X row shows the number X will use.
The X count is lower than the character count
A long link is in your text. X replaces it with a 23-character short link, so it counts as 23.
Use "Copy for Instagram (keep blank lines)". It puts an invisible Braille blank character on each empty line so Instagram keeps the gap.
YouTube does not allow angle brackets in titles or descriptions. Replace them with words or other symbols.
Some apps count each part of a complex emoji or count line breaks differently. Leave a few characters spare when you are close to a limit.
